previousExperience: Student assistant in accounting at a Danish SME (18 months)
Summer internship at an audit firm before the master's
case01.jobRoute: LinkedIn application to an English-speaking finance team
case01.challenges: Many finance roles asked for fluent Danish, and my first 15 applications to banks got no reply.
case01.strategy: I stopped applying to Danish-language roles and targeted large companies with English-speaking group finance teams. My student job manager became my strongest reference.
case01.story: I came to Denmark for my master's and worked part-time in a small accounting team. The job was not glamorous, but it taught me Danish bookkeeping practices and gave me concrete examples for interviews.
case01.advice: Relevant student experience mattered more than perfect Danish. Treat your student job as your first real job.

previousExperience: Research assistant at a university lab (1 year)
Portfolio of data projects using Danish open energy data
case02.jobRoute: Application through the company career page
case02.challenges: I had no network in Denmark and my generic applications were ignored for months.
case02.strategy: I built two public projects analysing Danish electricity prices and wind production, and linked them at the top of my CV. Interviewers asked about the projects in every interview.
case02.story: My CV looked like every other data science graduate's. Once I showed work on data the companies actually cared about, conversations became much easier.
case02.advice: A public GitHub with two solid, relevant projects opened more doors than my CV.

previousExperience: Marketing intern at a fashion start-up
Student job in a Copenhagen café (2 years)
case03.challenges: Marketing roles often need Danish copywriting, so I competed with native speakers.
case03.strategy: I invested in Danish classes up to B1 and positioned myself as the person who could run international campaigns while understanding the Danish market.
case03.story: My café job taught me how Danish customers talk and what they care about. A classmate who worked at the brand told me about the opening before it was posted.
case03.advice: Investing in B1 Danish helped me stand out from other internationals, and tell your network what you are looking for.

previousExperience: Summer internship at a boutique consultancy
Finalist in a university case competition
case04.challenges: Case interviews were completely new to me and I failed my first two.
case04.strategy: I joined a case-practice group and practised over 30 cases before the main recruiting round, focusing on structured communication.
case04.story: I applied to few firms but prepared intensively for each one. The case competition gave me something concrete to talk about.
case04.advice: Practise at least 30 cases before your first round of interviews.

previousExperience: Backend developer intern at a fintech company
Regular contributor to an open source payments library
case05.jobRoute: A recruiter reached out on LinkedIn
case05.challenges: I worried that not speaking Danish would rule me out of most companies.
case05.strategy: I focused on English-first tech companies and kept my LinkedIn and GitHub updated so recruiters could find me.
case05.story: My open source contributions showed that I could work in a real codebase with other developers, which mattered more than my grades.
case05.advice: Danish is not a blocker in tech. English-first companies exist here; make yourself easy to find.

previousExperience: Sales student assistant at a SaaS company
Exchange semester in Denmark during the bachelor's
case06.jobRoute: Direct application after meeting the team at an industry event
case06.challenges: Online applications rarely led anywhere, even with good Danish.
case06.strategy: I went to industry events and meetups in Aarhus, introduced myself in person and followed up with a short message the next day.
case06.story: An economics degree does not usually lead to sales, but my student job showed me I liked talking to customers. Moving to Aarhus gave me less competition.
case06.advice: Show up in person at industry events. Danes remember faces.

previousExperience: Freelance UX projects for three small businesses
Design internship at an Aarhus agency
case07.challenges: My early portfolio showed screens, not the thinking behind them, and I got generic rejections.
case07.strategy: I rebuilt my portfolio around two case studies describing the problem, research, iterations and results.
case07.story: My background is in humanities, so I had to prove I could design. Small freelance projects gave me real users and real results to show.
case07.advice: A tight portfolio with two case studies beats a long CV every time.

previousExperience: Student developer in the university IT department
Thesis on cloud architecture for a public organisation
case08.challenges: I started applying late and missed most graduate programme deadlines in my first round.
case08.strategy: I made a spreadsheet of graduate programmes and their deadlines and applied six months ahead for the next intake.
case08.story: The long search was frustrating, but my student developer job gave me practical examples of explaining technical problems to non-technical colleagues.
case08.advice: Apply to graduate programmes early. Deadlines close about six months before start.

case09.degree: MSc Operations and Supply Chain Management
previousExperience: Student job in a logistics warehouse (2 years)
Master's thesis on inventory optimisation written with a manufacturing company
case09.jobRoute: Hired by the company where I wrote my thesis
case09.challenges: Outside Copenhagen there were fewer international roles, and I had no contacts in industry.
case09.strategy: I contacted companies directly to propose a thesis collaboration. Working on their real data for five months turned into a job offer.
case09.story: Warehouse work taught me how operations look on the floor. That practical understanding made my thesis recommendations realistic, and the managers noticed.
case09.advice: Use your thesis as a five-month job interview. Write it with a company you would like to work for.

previousExperience: Three years as a mechanical engineer in production before the master's
Student assistant in a digital transformation team
case10.jobRoute: LinkedIn post about my career change followed by coffee meetings
case10.challenges: As a career changer I struggled to explain why an engineer wanted a business role, and my CV did not fit either category.
case10.strategy: I rewrote my story around solving process problems with data, which connected my engineering years with my new skills, and asked ten people for informal coffee meetings.
case10.story: I changed direction in my thirties. My production experience turned out to be an advantage, because I understood how the operations people I now work with think.
case10.advice: Do not hide a career change. Connect your old experience to the new role in one clear sentence.

previousExperience: Volunteer energy advisor in a student climate organisation
Internship analysing energy data for a municipality
case11.jobRoute: Referral from someone I met in my Danish language class
case11.challenges: Sustainability is popular, so entry-level roles received hundreds of applicants.
case11.strategy: I learned the new EU reporting requirements in depth and mentioned concrete regulations in my applications. A classmate from Danish class introduced me to her manager.
case11.story: My volunteering looked like a hobby on paper, but it gave me experience explaining technical topics to ordinary people, which is a big part of consulting.
case11.advice: Language classes are also networking. Talk to everyone there about what you do.

previousExperience: Volunteer with a newcomer integration project (2 years)
Student job in a municipal administration
case12.challenges: NGO jobs were few and usually required both Danish and field experience.
case12.strategy: I sent a short unsolicited application describing one concrete project I could help with, based on their annual report.
case12.story: Volunteering and a student job in the municipality taught me how Danish public systems work, which made my Danish improve quickly as well.
case12.advice: Unsolicited applications work in Denmark if you are specific about what you can do for them.

previousExperience: Hospitality student job in a hotel reception
Part-time customer support agent at the same company
case13.jobRoute: Converted from student worker to full-time after graduation
case13.challenges: I did not have a typical business background and was unsure which roles fit my communication degree.
case13.strategy: I took a part-time support job during my studies, proved myself, and asked about full-time openings six months before graduating.
case13.story: Years in hospitality taught me to stay calm with frustrated people. In customer success that turned out to be one of the most valued skills.
case13.advice: A student job inside the right company can be your fastest route to a full-time role.

previousExperience: Student assistant in a bank's compliance department
Teaching assistant in statistics
case14.challenges: Danish banks required Danish for most roles, so in my first year I could not apply.
case14.strategy: I committed to Danish lessons from day one and reached C1 over three years, while getting banking experience through a student job.
case14.story: Learning Danish was slow and expensive in time, but it opened the whole banking sector to me rather than a handful of English roles.
case14.advice: If your target industry works in Danish, start learning early. It compounds.
